A characterization of finite-dimensional commuting squares of C*-algebras, resulting in hyperfinite type II_1 subfactors of finite index and depth, is provided, utilizing Morita equivalent unitary fusion categories. We extend a prior investigation by N. Sato, generalizing his findings to encompass the broader context of such squares. Additionally, we establish a characterization for such squares yielding a given type II_1 subfactor, and this analysis contributes to a broader understanding of 4-tensors related to matrix product operators in 2-dimensional topological systems.

In this work, we introduce a novel meta-learning framework centered on ODE neural networks, which acquires an understanding of gradients. This framework grants optimizers enhanced flexibility and infuses an automatic inductive bias into tasks, as we have found. Through the simplest Hamiltonian Neural Network implementation, our method proves more effective than a comparable LSTM-based meta-learner for a simulated task and MNIST with ReLU activations for a continuous task, as we have found.

A critical issue with using machine learning systems is assessing their dependability, as they can have severe consequences. One method to evaluate a machine learning system's reliability is to introduce a score that signifies its credibility. Building upon this idea, we've created a system called TrustLoop, which is a multi-agent setup designed to calculate a score that signifies the credibility of a machine learning model in real-time. As new data is fed into the model, a set of machine learning detectors identify and flag any suspicious data, which is then used to create a new dataset for a clustering algorithm. The resulting features from this process are combined with a score that signifies the credibility of the model and is presented to a human user who decides on the reliability of the model. We conducted a study with a machine learning system that predicts whether a tweet is written in Spanish or Galician, and found that TrustLoop increases confidence in the model's accuracy by 10% when it identifies suspicious data, according to our experimental results.

In x-ray image analysis, identifying prohibited items holds significant importance for ensuring public safety in various fields, including airport and cargo security inspections. While existing research has primarily concentrated on refining recognition algorithms, very little has been done to examine the real-world feasibility and performance of such algorithms. In order to evaluate the real-world potential of xxl-xray, a high-quality benchmark has been developed, consisting of four components: comprehensive data annotations, a set of evaluation metrics accounting for inter-class dependencies, a protocol for assessing the realistic proponent class setup, and a baseline model featuring a lateral inhibition module that considers neighboring information. Furthermore, to explore various scenarios, an advanced model with a multi-scale cross attention block has been introduced. Comparative results have indicated that these methods outperform current mainstream algorithms on the real-world x-ray image dataset, with improvements in F1-score ranging from 10% to 40% in several evaluations, demonstrating the effectiveness of the introduced methods.

A newly defined polynomial, referred to as the nth toroidal colored Jones polynomial, is established for links in a thickened torus. By deriving a specialized differential operator, the proof proves that the nth toroidal colored Jones polynomial of a link can be obtained by applying the operator n times to the Alexander polynomial of the link's projection on the torus. Consequently, the limit volume behavior of the Conjectured Volume for the polynomial is proofed with an upper limit.

The primary objective of Word Sense Disambiguation (WSD) involves determining the appropriate sense of a word with multiple meanings within a particular context.  Advances in deep learning, specifically utilizing BERT, have led to significant progress in this area, with several strategies being developed to combine structured knowledge, particularly in the form of word glosses, with contextual information to achieve even greater improvements.  A simple yet effective method is proposed to extend the context of a word, complementing an existing approach that incorporates word glosses; this method is termed "context-gloss augmentation" and is shown to be particularly beneficial for low-frequency words with a limited frequency in training data.  The proposed approach is evaluated through extensive experimentation on the Multi20 New York Times Corpus (Multi20NYT), demonstrating its superiority to alternative methods, with notable gains in micro-F1 score achieved, including a 15.4% improvement when using context-gloss augmented context with a BERT-based baseline and feature selection model.

This study formulates a genuine integral expression of the reciprocal gamma function in terms of a modified hypersingular integral. It also proves the connection to the traditional complex representation, in addition to obtaining a modified complex representation following the standard Hankel path.

The CMS experiment at the CERN LHC detected the production of top quarks for the first time using data from proton-lead interactions at a 5.02 TeV nucleon-nucleon center-of-mass energy. Top quark production was identified in data with an integrated luminosity of 185$\,\mu$b and an energy scale of 800 GeV, specifically searching for events featuring one isolated electron isolated from hadrons, accompanied by multiple isolated photons. These signatures distinguish themselves from background signals due to the characteristic $e\gamma$ invariant mass distribution. Measured values for the top quark signal yield and cross-section were found to be 32 $\pm$ 4 (statistical uncertainty) $\pm$ 9 (systematic uncertainty) and 69.9 $\pm$ 7.4 (statistical uncertainty) $\pm$ 10.9 (systematic uncertainty) nb, respectively, in agreement with theoretical predictions within 1.5 standard deviations. Additionally, results were compared to proton-proton predictions, taking into account the influence of nuclear effects.

This study focuses on key elements in cross-domain text-to-SQL parsing, specifically schema linking and value filling. To enhance encoding abilities, a column selection auxiliary task is proposed, leveraging explicit targets for relevance matching. Additionally, two value filling approaches are presented to bridge the gap between current zero-shot parsers and practical applications, considering that many existing parsers overlook value filling in synthesized SQL. Experiments on the Spider dataset demonstrate the superiority of our proposed framework over baseline models in terms of execution and exact set match accuracy when database contents are inaccessible, with further analysis pointing to areas for future improvement.

This paper delves into the utilization of differential privacy within the framework of graph-based data. It outlines the DP formulations relevant to publishing graphs, extracting patterns from graphs, and generating synthetic data based on graph properties. Additionally, it examines DP-compatible machine learning techniques for motif discovery and graph generation. Given the absence of a comprehensive survey on this topic, particularly in light of recent advancements in DP-compatible machine learning on graph data, this work serves as a foundational DP framework for future research in graph-based data mining.

The vast amount of images, data, and resources that Euclid will generate positions the consortium to create comprehensive legacy databases with significant longevity. To capitalize on this potential, the Euclid legacy community has been established to formulate strategies for exploiting these resources. This community will outline the scientific potential of various secondary analyses based on the primary science goals that Euclid achieves.

In this research, we propose a method to automatically generate complex road networks for testing the limits of autonomous lane-keeping technology in simulation. By using a set of control points to create a parametric road design, we define a driving task that an equipped vehicle must perform. Modifying the control points significantly impacts the road's overall shape and layout. Our approach leverages optimization techniques to identify a set of control points that creates challenging driving conditions, causing the vehicle to deviate from its programmed course. We validated our method with three distinct search configurations, focusing on balancing testing speed and practicality for simulated evaluations of autonomous lane-keeping systems.

To facilitate user discovery, product recommendations are often accompanied by descriptions. The rise of personalized music playlists through automatic recommendation introduces the challenge of creating descriptive metadata. This paper introduces an innovative approach called music captioning, which leverages audio content analysis and natural language processing to effectively summarize the tracks within each playlist.

Researchers have successfully used hydrodynamic theories to simulate complex dynamics in bosonic mixtures, drawing a connection to experimental observations. Building upon this success, a stochastic hydrodynamic approach is now proposed, incorporating quantum effects and successfully deriving the classical stochastic hydrodynamics as a limiting case. This new framework extends the simulation capabilities to binary Bose gases by deriving a phase-space stochastic hydrodynamic (P-SHiP) equation that incorporates two-body interactions, and demonstrating its link to the exact master equation in the limiting case of low densities.

Temporal action detection is focused on pinpointing the start and end points of actions within a video. A key challenge lies in accurately segmenting diverse actions, taking into account the temporal context. To address this, we propose DCAN, a DC-compatible context aggregation network that extracts local details and temporal side information. This allows for effective aggregation of context features from both ends, resulting in a comprehensive contextual representation. Specifically, we utilize a dilated convolutional convolutional structure to capture extensive information without compromising sampling rates, and incorporate a direction-sensitive temporal aggregation module to combine background context from both directions. Experiments conducted on two widely recognized benchmark datasets, TVR-Action and DW-Action, demonstrate the superiority of our method, achieving state-of-the-art performance.

The long-lived palm tree modes (PTM) found in the JET tokamak's edge plasma remain controversial due to their unexplained rotation dynamics. A recently discovered class of edge localized modes in the JET tokamak has shown remarkable similarity to palm tree structures in Edge Localization Mode Probability Scans, particularly in rotation frequency. Further analysis using multiple rotation frequency data sets and spatial density data sets has shown that some edge modes share characteristics with PTMs. Notably, these similar edge modes exhibit rotation frequency and direction patterns, as well as life span durations comparable to their PTM counterparts. However, they differ in persistence and lack the multi-second life span of typical palm tree modes. Their flat top life phase suggests that a localized mode with sustained balance between dissipation and pumping may form the basis of PTMs.

This research focuses on resolving collision avoidance for non-holonomic robots moving at constant speeds in a 2D space, leveraging dynamic vortex potential fields. A new class of vector fields is introduced to model the behavior, with a specific derivation for the fields given under certain constraints. It is shown through analysis that the fields result in a stable equilibrium where the equilibrium's type varies based on the relative positions of the agents, with outcomes including non-collisions, head-on collisions, and safe passage, all illustrated with simulations.

Given an independent and identically distributed sequence of letters, a large deviation principle for the frequency of letters within an sequence of words has been thoroughly studied. In contrast, determining large deviation principles for sequences of words constructed from letter sequences that follow an independent Markov chain of order $m$ poses a challenge. This study establishes that when the letters are generated by such Markov chains, especially when they only need to be of order $m \geq 2k-1$ (where $k$ denotes the length of words), modified versions of the large deviation principle for independent letters apply. Furthermore, it is shown that if the underlying Markov chain is of a lower order $m < 2k-1$ (but excluding $m=k-1$), significant savings in memory are achievable without significantly altering large deviation behavior for sequences of words constructed from such letters.

Recent advancements in wireless communications have led to the development of large-scale Intelligent Reflecting Surface (IRS) systems that can dynamically adjust the propagation path between a radar and its target. By utilizing an IRS, the scale of range bin ambiguity is significantly reduced due to the enhanced reflection coefficients and path differences, thus providing more accurate target parameter estimates. In this work, we investigate the potential of IRS systems to improve target parameter estimation accuracy in monostatic radar configurations, and introduce a novel concept known as Large Scale Ambiguity Virtualization (LSAV). Through theoretical analysis and simulations, our results show that with the implementation of an IRS system, the estimated target range and velocity will converge to their actual values as the IRS system scale increases, whereas without an IRS system, this convergence does not occur. In addition, our work reveals that with an IRS system, there exists an optimal intermediate velocity at which the estimated velocity equals its actual value. In the absence of an IRS system, the estimated range and velocity are limited by their respective Nyquist scales, which are significantly smaller than the large scale ambiguities of the radar system. As the radar system scale grows, the Nyquist scale ambiguity becomes smaller than the large scale ambiguity, and with the introduction of an IRS system, the target parameter estimation accuracy is expected to be improved.

Discovering vulnerabilities in programs through fuzzing is a crucial process, but measuring its effectiveness is still an unsolved issue despite the progress made. A widely accepted evaluation standard in software testing is mutation analysis, assessing the ability to detect artificial flaws, and has led to several comparisons of testing tools for static analysis, slicing, and reaching. However, no similar framework exists for evaluating and comparing the effectiveness of fuzzers. This paper introduces the first platform for assessing and comparing the potential of fuzzers in finding vulnerabilities, and also presents initial results from a study that evaluated three popular fuzzers: AFL, AFLfast, and AFLang. The findings show that the fuzzer's performance is measured by the vulnerabilities it uncovers, and certain advantages of using mutation score or reachability score over just counting unique instructions are demonstrated. Additionally, the conclusion that comparing fuzzers using the vulnerability corpus is more reliable than using program properties is drawn.

Following the success of pre-trained models in various tasks, numerous techniques have been developed to adapt them for continual learning scenarios. Nonetheless, no comprehensive analysis has been conducted on how these methods compare to more basic approaches that also utilize pre-trained models. Our research fills this gap by examining a range of continual learning strategies that build upon popular frameworks like Model Averaging and Progressive Neural Networks. We designed and executed a large-scale experiment with 30 tasks, comparing our approaches to several baseline models that employ pre-trained models through repeat, average, and sequential applications. Our findings reveal that our methods perform on par with, and in some cases better than, prominent continual learning algorithms like LTN and Dual-Optimization. Notably, our results indicate that the use of pre-trained models makes even a more limited strategy, such as Model Averaging, highly effective. Consequently, the use of pre-trained models appears to be a more impactful factor than the complex designs of specific algorithms, raising concerns that the current evaluation metrics for continual learning methods, which heavily rely on pre-trained models, need to be re-examined.

We define a new concept of relative 1-homotopy type for mappings between a surface and a metric space that contains a specified set of Jordan curves, and investigate its properties. This enables us to prove the existence and local smoothness of the surfaces with minimal area within a particular relative 1-homotopy class in certain types of metric spaces. Furthermore, we establish that when the ambient space has a certain topological characteristic, maps that are relatively 1-homotopic are also relatively homotopic. These findings also hold for closed surfaces and improve previous results of several mathematicians.

This final installment concludes our comprehensive study of the solution $u$ to the given heat equation on the real line. Specifically, we analyze instances where solutions converge in local compact sets to potentially different heat equations' solutions at positive infinity and minus infinity, based on Local Uniform Conjecture. The initial data $u_0$ in this case consists of locally bounded, nonnegative functions declining to zero at both infinity points. While cases of identical limits at both infinity were covered in our earlier work, this paper focuses on scenarios with distinct limits at infinity, particularly heat equations solutions with limits zero at minus infinity and $A$ at plus infinity, where $A$ is non-zero. Additionally, we extend investigation to instances where the data has a finite norm in $L^1(\mathbb{R})$.

Recent studies on the 64Ni nucleus with a low-spin structure have made significant progress using modern anangular Drift Detectors, in particular, a study using 40Ca projectiles at 350 MeV has significantly improved resolution. As a result, a complex pattern of energy levels has been identified that suggests a pair of 0+ nuclei with significant overlap. A theoretical model based on the Interacting Boson-Shell Model successfully defines the nucleus' structure, in particular, two distinct shapes, normal and octupole, characterized by specific configurations.

Approximately nine years ago, Azrieli and Shmaya introduced a category of $\lambda$-Lipschitz games where each player's payoff function is influenced by a $\lambda$-Lipschitz rate in response to other players' actions. These games were initially found to have the property of achieving $\Omega(\sqrt{\lambda})$-$\epsilon$-support size balanced queries (SBQs) for $O(\epsilon^4/\lambda^2)$ improvement since then, in 2015, Rubinstein provided a clearer demonstration using SBQs, employing an $\Omega(\sqrt{\lambda})$ query lower bound that aligned closely with the current best-known outcomes for equilibrium finding (within the given class of Lipschitz games) under balanced queries.

Machine learning models often undergo performance assessment through k-fold cross-validation to facilitate model selection and parameter adjustment. Yet, due to the substantial computational demands of machine learning models, particularly in natural language processing (NLP), conducting multiple runs is not always feasible. This paper delves into the statistical underpinnings of using K-J x K-K fold cross-validation over a single run with a large K value. Our analysis reveals that as K increases, the variance of the estimate of expected accuracy rises. Instead, our proposed J-K x K-K fold approach keeps the variance at comparable levels while allowing the experiment to be conducted with a more manageable K value. Furthermore, we provide guidance on optimal parameter choices for this strategy. The effectiveness of using the J-K x K-K fold approach is demonstrated through statistical tests and illustrative plots.

Deep Neural Networks have achieved remarkable success, yet they are computationally costly to train. To mitigate this, Teacher-Student architectures have been widely adopted, with significant research on Teacher knowledge transfer already conducted primarily in specific domains like NLP and computer vision. However, a comprehensive study on Teacher-Student architectures across various fields was missing. This study aims to bridge this gap by providing a thorough examination of Teacher-Student architectures, with an emphasis on the underlying knowledge transfer mechanisms and the development of transfer strategies. Furthermore, this research explores emerging trends like curriculum learning and knowledge distillation mechanisms, as well as potential areas for future investigation. With an index that facilitates easy navigation, this research provides a user-friendly guide for academics and practitioners working in knowledge transfer using Teacher-Student architectures.

We introduce a new efficient framework for representing functions in the context of conditional optimization and discrete game-playing in graphical models. Our framework is based on exact, closed-form expressions using standard mathematical functions, which significantly reduce computational complexity. This new efficiency in computing function values translates to a substantial acceleration of a recently introduced exact algorithm for finding perfect equilibria in games, known as the global optimisation approach. When applied to certain classes of Bayesian networks, the enhanced computational efficiency of our framework allows the exact computation of perfect equilibria in linear time relative to the number of variables in the network. Furthermore, our framework is adaptable to games with constrained objective functions. The practical benefits of our approach are demonstrated through comparative performance results with the state-of-the-art local-method-based FPOU on a range of Bayesian network-based constrained optimisation problems.

We investigated the absorption of a single, monochromatic light beam at 689 nm in a monatomic strontium gas that has been cooled to extremely low temperatures. When researchers integrated the signal from this absorption spectroscopy, they found that the ratio of atomic transitions per photon absorbed varied significantly, ranging from less than one to more than one. This ratio was observed to change as the atomic velocity with respect to the light beam's frequency changed. A new theoretical model successfully described this relationship, taking into account the effects of the light beam on the atoms' absorption patterns. This model can be utilized to refine velocity-selectated fluorescence spectroscopy, a technique that has been recently developed.

When subjected to high stresses, the vast majority of dense mixtures experience a sudden shift from free-flowing to rigid behavior, a phenomenon known as shear thickening. A hypothesis has emerged that transitions marked by shear thickening exhibit universal properties, similar to other material phase transitions. This study delves into a specific example of this hypothesis by analyzing the point at which discontinuous shear thickening occurs in volumes of silica particles mixed with glycerol. Instead, we plot the critical stress needed to trigger this transition against the volume fraction of particles, using the distance from the random close packing fraction as our measure of control variable. We then observe that all our data points converge to a single curve, indicating that distinct transitions can in fact share a common underlying pattern.

Recently introduced is a higher rank algebra known as the Racah algebra $R(n)$. A special variant, termed the special Racah algebra $sR(n)$, is then defined as a quotient of the Racah algebra by its central elements. It is then demonstrated that this $sR(n)$ algebra is equivalent to the centralizer $Z_{n}(\mathfrak{sl}_2)$ through application of classical invariant theory. Furthermore, we derive an explicit formula for the central elements of the Racah algebra $R(n)$ through the use of character theory and recursive relations, which in turn enables determination of the special Racah algebra $sR(n)$ in specific instances. It is also established that the Hilbert-Poincar\'e series of the centralizer $Z_{n}(\mathfrak{sl}_2)$ mirrors that of the centralizer $Z_{n}(\mathfrak{sp}_{2m})$ discovered by Zhong and Zhang.

Our study reveals that in a bilayer Heisenberg antiferromagnet, low-lying triplon excitations can give rise to twisted superfluid and supersolid phases, which are novel quantum states that have not been observed in magnetic systems previously.  Using a DMRG approach, we find that magnetic supersolids arise from the interaction of triplons, which contrasts with the non-magnetic supersolid phase typically seen in quantum many-body systems.  Our L-SGM findings show that twisted supersolid phases can be understood through a Ginzburg-Landau theory, which also provides a link between twisted superfluid and supersolid phases.  We demonstrate that twisted supersolid phases can be stabilized by a combination of interlayer dimer interactions and a triplon-mediated interlayer Heisenberg interaction, with the degree of twist in the triplon order being controlled by the ratio of these interactions.  Additionally, we show that an interlayer transverse field can induce a twisted Mott triplon insulating phase, which serves as a connection between twisted supersolid and twisted Mott insulating phases.  Using a VUMC method, we find that our two-layer model can also be realized in the A-type vanadate perovskite materials, with a narrow band triplon Mott-Leggett mode potentially being detectable via inelastic neutron scattering.  However, we also show that a more directly realizable system is a dimerized

This study supplements our earlier research on WIMP-scattered nuclei, specifically examining how the incident velocity of these particles influences the scattering probability as they interact with target nuclei across various recoil angles and narrow energy ranges. Our simulation reveals that not only do the incident velocity characteristics of halo WIMPs play a crucial role, but so does the angle of the recoil itself. Furthermore, under the halo assumption, our findings contradict initial predictions made by the simplified formula of the WIMP velocity distribution, which had inaccurately estimated the incident velocity distribution within a specific, small range of energies. As a result, this flawed prediction led to an overestimation of the associated angular recoil-Energy spectra. Our research also highlights the significant impact of the scattering cross-section's geometric factor in determining the angular recoil-Energy spectrum, a critical consideration overlooked under the naive assumption. Based on our in-depth analysis of the scattering process, we derived a more accurate, process-based formula for calculating the incident velocity distribution, which was found to be 2 orders of magnitude lower than the flawed prediction made by the basic formula of the WIMP velocity distribution.

An estimated 90 percent of the world's population relies on Google's Web search as their primary source of information, which has evolved into a significant public good. However, the extent to which algorithms like Google's Web search efficiently achieve this status remains unclear. As a prominent example, the personalisation of search results based on individual user profiles may lead to significant subsets of relevant information being consistently overlooked and thus, missed by a substantial number of users. A series of experiments was conducted to test this hypothesis, involving 180 participants who used Google's Web search to locate all relevant options in three distinct choice-based tasks. The frequency with which participants failed to identify all relevant alternatives was recorded and compared to simulated instances where the same tasks were performed without the use of a search engine. The surprising findings revealed that, according to Google's Web search data, 40 percent of relevant alternatives were consistently missed by these users, which was also 39 percent higher than in the no-search scenarios. This evidence highlights the need to consider search engine algorithms carefully, given the significant impact they can have on how we access and process crucial information.

We are suggesting the establishment of a state-of-the-art muon-proton and muon-nucleus collider that operates at the TeV level, capable of delivering highly accurate measurements in deep inelastic scattering in new areas, while also offering a comprehensive research agenda in particle and nuclear physics. By doing so, we believe it could either drive the advancement or make use of existing particle accelerators, specifically taking advantage of established infrastructure if constructed at places like Brookhaven National Laboratory, Fermilab, or CERN. In this concept, we outline various design parameters for several collider configurations and evaluate potential for scientific discoveries with these designs.

A novel approach to combining large respiratory motion compensation and motion encoding in four-dimensional MRI scans is introduced. This method utilizes a dual-echo, four-dimensional MRI sequence based on the spin-echo technique, which can capture high-resolution images of the abdomen and pelvis region. The sequence employs a respiratory bellows system to collect data and compensates for respiratory motion in three dimensions using a linear predictive model. The dual-echo sequence acquires two sets of images with different readout readout lengths, which are then combined into a single, motion-compensated image set through an interpolation technique. A clinical trial utilizing this sequence on six healthy volunteers demonstrated its effectiveness in compensating for respiratory motion and producing high-resolution images with a readout resolution of 1.4 mm. The sequence's ability to compensate for motion and provide clear images in a short scan time of less than 10 minutes makes it a promising technique for clinical use.

This research paper proposes a novel approach to developing safety-critical controllers for complex nonlinear control systems subject to input limitations. Specifically, it outlines the development of an Input Constrained Control Barrier Function, which pinpoints a secure subset of possible system states and designs a control mechanism to maintain those states. The devised controller can be optimized through an efficiently solvable quadratic program, enabling real-time application. Building upon earlier concepts of Higher Order Control Barrier Functions, ICCBFs demonstrate the ability to tackle a broader class of systems characterized by variable relative degrees. Finally, the paper showcases its efficacy through simulation examples in adaptive cruise control and spacecraft rendezvous.

In this work, domains are represented by equipping certain subsets of a set with a special structure, specifically an approximation space. Initially, we define domain-like structures via CF-approximation spaces, and subsequently, we prove that any domain can be represented by a CF-approximation space. Finally, we investigate the properties of CF-approximation spaces that allow for interdomain mappings.

The paired-permutation test in NLP systems has long relied on approximate methods, such as the randomization or asymptotic distribution, to estimate the p-value. In contrast, our research offers an innovative, exact algorithm for computing the p-value in paired-permutation testing, particularly for when test statistics adhere to addition and comparison rules. This algorithm is executed efficiently through parallel processing, and when combined with sufficient computational resources, allows for the exact determination of p-values.

A comprehensive dataset of freight rates, shipping quantities, new ship prices, used ship prices, and scrapped ship prices has been assembled for the container shipping sector from 1966 to 2014. Unfortunately, public access to this high-quality dataset is currently limited. Further research should focus on unlocking the potential of this dataset to benefit the container shipping industry and related fields. Notably, the container shipping industry is characterized by its global integration, extensive use of technology, and significant influence on international trade and shipping. As a result, it serves as an ideal setting for examining the application of containerization to highly interconnected, technologically advanced markets in the context of globalization.

We define loom spaces as a more general framework incorporating leaf spaces for pseudo-Anosov flows and link spaces for veering triangulations. Building on Gu\'eritaud's research, it is demonstrated that there is a veering triangulation inherently linked to every loom space, with this triangulation's realization being topologically equivalent to 3D space.

Graph neural networks have excelled in various applications, but their intricate structures hinder users from comprehending how they function. To address this issue, research has focused on enhancing the interpretability of these models. One promising approach involves simplifying the underlying graph by selectively removing edges, thereby making the model's operations more transparent. By fine-tuning Graph neural networks, the objective is to maintain similar performance while maximizing the sparsification of the underlying graph. This research extends the fine-tuning framework by generalizing the sparsification objective to accommodate various forms of edge removal. The proposed framework leads to the exception of Edge Pruned Graph Neural Networks, a focused algorithm that seamlessly integrates the graph learning capabilities of popular neural network architectures. The proposed method demonstrates the capability of significantly pruning edges from the underlying graph without compromising model performance, and delivers superior results compared to the state-of-the-art baselines in the interpretability research.

A well-known dimensionality reduction technique called CountSketch employs randomized linear measurements to map vectors from a high-dimensional space into a lower-dimensional space. Under the assumption of sparse vectors unknown to the designer, CountSketch effectively reconstructs the original vector from its measurements. However, in a scenario where the counting sketch is subjected to adversarial input, it is possible for distinct high-dimensional vectors to produce the same output subspace, rendering count sketching inconclusive. We enhance the initial analysis by providing the precise condition under which adversarial vectors can be effectively compressed into a specific low-dimensional space, from which a CountSketch-type decoder can identify the most likely original vector based on its sparsity. Additionally, we develop a more robust alternative code in the form of a randomized binary signing scheme, which, when combined with the unknown sparse vector, yields a compressed version that allows for effective reconstruction. The proposed code demonstrates resilience against an adversary and achieves the same optimal compression performance as CountSketch, requiring the same number of measurements in the ideal scenario.

Building on previous findings, we observed in Part I that compact, singular areas within a manifold of positive scalar curvature can be conformally deformed to reveal related minimal geometries sharing key characteristics. This deformation preserves features like Ahlfors regularity, Poincare inequality validity, and tangent cones with positive scalar curvature. In Part II, we employ surgery-style arguments to successfully remove the singular sets present in these geometries.

A liquid composed of superconducting vortices exhibits non-equilibrium properties reminiscent of complex, irreversibly damaged materials. This composition contains two distinct phases - a dynamic component representing motionless, freely moving charge carriers that contribute to the non-equilibrium entropy and a static component in the form of a pinned, interlocked pile of vortures that behaves like a rigid body with two types of viscosity - internal friction among the pinned vortices and Mondon-Landau-Lifshitz (Muller) forces acting between the vortex piles. This dynamic-mixed phase displays a unique form of Nernst response, characterized by the liquid's ability to convert a temperature gradient across the material into a magnetic field, with the resulting field being proportional to the product of the entropy and the static component's viscosity, with the result being most prominent near a second-order phase transition, with the resulting values of the Nernst coefficient approaching the ratio of the Planck constant to the charge carrier's charge, with the Nernst coefficient of the vortex liquid exceeding that of the pinned vortices by a factor of the ratio of the boiling point to the critical temperature, with the result explaining the unique behavior of the normal state in type-II superconducting liquids under high pressure and in heavy-fermion superconductors.

Effective management of controllable loads relies on the strategic use of aggregate flexibility, which encapsulates the feasible future control options within a predictable framework. This framework is crucial for developing predictive control strategies that optimize specific objectives and ensure desired performance outcomes. This paper introduces a novel method using machine learning to efficiently solve complex optimization problems, thereby establishing a robust foundation for design and performance guarantees in predictive control systems. The efficiency and accuracy of the proposed approach are demonstrated through the implementation of a real-world predictive control application for municipal electricity distribution networks.

The recent rise of high-frequency trading has driven up the complexity of
stock price forecasting. Using historical data alone to predict prices is an
increasingly difficult task. This project combines deep learning techniques,
specifically GANs and a BERT-based encoder, to enhance the accuracy of
stock price prediction. We employ a BERT encoder to predict the next closing
price and a GAN, consisting of a discriminator and generator, to refine the
predictions by trying to predict and generate real data respectively.

One of the most intriguing phenomena in astrophysics is the common envelope (CE) phase, which occurs when a novabinary, superbinary, or similar binary system's wind causes mass loss. This process results in one or both stars being engulfed, leading to a complex interaction between wind, mass, and spiral arms that can trigger the CE phase. Despite being involved in some of the most compact binary sources, such as X-ray novae, merger products, and supernovae, the nature of the CE phase and its implications remain poorly understood. To address this, a new, unified model for the CE phase is proposed, which encompasses various sources and defines distinct stages of binary evolution that can result in compact sources, mergers, or CE phases. This model demonstrates that during the CE phase, there are three primary components (engulfed primary star, secondary star, and inner disk) that exist in a dynamic equilibrium, where mass and momentum are redistributed among these components, which is the key to surviving the CE phase. This model is compared to alternative scenarios, such as the CE phase in some X-ray novae, certain superbinary mergers, and some supernovae, to demonstrate the implications of the new common envelope model.

This research investigates double Higgs boson production at future electron-positron colliders CLIC and ILC with TeV-scale energies, considering the Effective Field Theory (EFT) to study BSM interactions. Higgs boson production processes, specifically $e^+e^-\to \gamma\gamma \to HH$, $\gamma Z \to HH$, and hadronically produced $WWWW \to HH$, are thoroughly examined with a focus on BBKK final states. By analyzing the sensitivity of the ClIC and ILC colliders through detailed simulations, the study highlights the potential for these machines to precisely measure the Higgs boson and its interactions with other Standard Model particles, particularly the W, Z, and BBK K forces. The Higgs factory nature of ClIC and ILC colliders offers a unique opportunity to precisely test the non-abelian nature of the Higgs boson and provides high sensitivity to the BSM interactions, with the ClIC colliders having the highest sensitivity to effectively double Higgs production.

We perform a covariant expansion of the Einstein-Hilbert action in powers of
$1/c^2$, considering a generic spacetime foliation defined by $c$, the speed
of light. We achieve this through the application of a suitable 'pre-non-
relativistic' geometrical parametrization, thereby facilitating an
analytical $1/c^2$ expansion of general relativity. Ultimately, this method
permits an in-depth examination of the Einstein-Hilbert action expansion up to
its next-to-next-to-leading order.

A new computational framework is introduced to speed up the calculation of localized shocks in a five-dimensional space that mimics anti-gravity, by simplifying the complex Einstein equations. It's discovered that using a first-order approximation yields highly accurate results, which can be broken down into two manageable sets of equations. Further, it's observed that one set has minimal impact on boundary measurements, allowing the calculation to be streamlined. This improvement results in significantly faster numerical solutions, with minimal errors, at roughly one-tenth the original time for specific conditions.

We investigated the drag experienced by a long cylindrical solid moving through a layer of granular material, specifically polycractic fractures, as it moved perpendicular to its long axis and in various directions relative to its long axis. The speed at which the cylinder moved and the orientation of its long axis affected the drag it experienced. This indicated that the movement of a solid through a layer of granular material depends on the direction in which it moves. This effect is referred to as drag anisotropy and is a significant factor to consider when studying how particles move through sediment. The relationship between the drag experienced by the cylinder and its movement could be described using equivalent linear drag coefficients that varied based on the direction of movement. This variation followed a predictable pattern. To better understand this phenomenon, we developed a theoretical model based on Darcy's law, which made assumptions about the flow of fluid around the cylinder. This model's results matched the drag observed in experiments very well. The variation in drag seen in these experiments is a significant effect that should be considered when evaluating the movement of particles through sediment. It is especially important in situations where particles are slow-moving, which is often the case for particles that are being moved by groundwater. This could have a significant effect on how particles are found in sediment and the geology that forms as layers of sediment build up. This is because the movement of particles is not uniform, which could result in the formation of concentrations of particles. This is evident in the results seen in

Using observations from KCWI, we studied how outflows interact with the interstellar medium in a starbursting galaxy, IC3528, by examining mass and momentum transfer, as well as energy transfer. Our analysis reveals that at sub-kiloparsec scales, outflows carry mass and momentum at rates consistent with those observed on larger scales. However, excessive sunlight reaches the gas within the galaxy's outer regions, potentially inhibiting future star formation due to over-irradiation. Although the outflows seem effective in regulating star formation, the sunlight-driven processes contribute more to this effect than the outflows do.

Current auto-tuning frameworks for computer systems face challenges in efficiently handling a large configuration space, especially when using a small training dataset due to the high cost of experimentation. Traditional methods like grid search, random search, and local search are limited by their inability to handle complex interactions between parameters effectively. Machine learning approaches, on the other hand, struggle to maintain a meaningful configuration space as parameters are increased in number. To address this issue, we introduce BoGraph, a novel structured Bayesian optimization framework that leverages a graph-based specification of the configuration space. BoGraph utilizes a graph model to guide its search, prune the space, and remove redundant parameters during optimization, and it guides its search using the semantics of graph transformations, and it prunes the space, removes redundant parameters during optimization, and it uses the graph model to learn from its experiments, and it uses a Markov random field, and it uses a graph model to learn from its experiments, and it uses a graph-based specification of the configuration space, and it uses a Markov random field, and it uses a graph model to learn from its experiments.

Our research examined the connection between initial anisotropic geometry and anisotropic flow within a multiphase transport model, specifically for 200 GeV Au+Au and Cu+Cu collisions. Contrary to elliptical flow's dependence on centrality, we discovered minimal variation in triangular flow centrality. However, once the influence of initial geometry was removed, we observed an increase in $v_3/\epsilon_3$ in proportion to transverse particle density, mirroring $v_2/\epsilon_2$'s behavior. Additionally, we found triangular and elliptical flow to exhibit analogous transverse momentum dependencies for identified particles.

Over the years, the availability of Linked Data has significantly expanded,
however, numerous challenges persist in ensuring its integration with web services
and subsequent interoperability. One major issue lies in the varying levels of
data integrity, as publicly accessible Data Sources (DSs) often suffer from
severe limitations in quality. To address this concern, we have devised a comprehensive
quality assessment procedure for Linked Data collections. This process involves
formulating appropriate queries to validate the values and structural integrity
of individual DSs, as well as examining the relationships and compatibility
between them. To enhance efficiency, we have implemented this process with
iterative,
semantic, and cross-source checks, leveraging a high-performance querying
system. This setup enables us to effectively evaluate the quality of large-scale
datasets, as demonstrated with real-world examples.

When working with data generated by random processes, an appropriate method for analyzing and predicting it is MLE. However, traditional likelihood-based techniques are not always applicable due to the complexity of likelihood functions, which often lack a closed-form expression. This paper introduces M-MLE, an innovative method for parameter estimation that overcomes these limitations by utilizing a robust likelihood estimator, making the approach suitable for a broader range of stochastic processes. The effectiveness of M-MLE is demonstrated through the use of an interest rate model, where the traditional Heston model is compared to a more complex process called the Cox-Ingersoll-Ross model with time-varying parameters. The results show that while the simpler Heston model can be adequately fitted using M-MLE, it is not the most appropriate model for the data, and the more complex process provides the best fit. The performance of M-MLE is also assessed through the use of Monte Carlo simulations and the analysis of the residual process of the observed data.

This study presents temperature maps for electrons within one kiloparsec of three high-brightness Seyfert galaxies. The findings from Gemini and VLT/FORS2 observations reveal temperature variations in these galaxies, with typical ranges between 10^4 to 10^5 Kelvin. Notably, the data show temperature anisotropy in all observed galaxies, with some regions exhibiting significantly higher or lower temperatures along different directions. In two out of three galaxies, distinct temperature patterns were identified, including counter-rotating disks and wide-line galaxies. Furthermore, the research highlights the presence of cold emission tails aligned with large-scale galaxy structures, suggesting that active galactic nuclei can shape wide structures beyond 500 parsecs. The implications of these temperature patterns for tuning theoretical models of active galactic nuclei interactions with their surrounding environments are discussed.

As IoT systems shift towards Edge computing and less reliable infrastructure closer to users, the working environment of IoT applications changes significantly. To ensure the seamless operation of these apps, it's crucial to address their reliability issues through effective testing. This concept of Device-Driven Testing aims to enhance the reliability of IoT apps by identifying and rectifying design flaws that arise from discrepancies between the intended and actual behavior of devices in these systems. The core idea involves creating test cases that examine the feasibility of software components' requirement specifications against real-world device behavior, utilizing evolvable test suites to facilitate iterative design improvements. A case study on the Climate Control System (CCS) IoT application demonstrates the potential of this approach and is further detailed on the associated website.

The ATLAS experiment at the Large Hadron Collider (LHC) has achieved precise measurements in two areas, namely neutral B meson mixing and CP violation, as well as in rare electroweak processes occurring in suppressed B-meson decays. This study concentrates on recent findings from the ATLAS collaboration, encompassing evaluations of rare occurrences like $B^0_s \to \mu^+\mu^-$ and $B^0 \to \mu^+\mu^-$ decays and the determination of CP-violating processes in $B^0_s \to J/\psi\phi$.

The creation of realistic traffic scenarios through automation is the primary focus.
Currently used approaches insert virtual characters into the environment using predefined rules but struggle to capture the complexity and variability of actual traffic conditions due to their reliance on simple modeling techniques.
As a result, these methods have limited applicability in thoroughly testing the performance of self-driving vehicles under a wide range of circumstances.
To address this shortcoming, we propose SceneGen, a traffic scene generation model based on artificial neural networks.
This model is trained to generate realistic traffic scenarios through statistical traffic data, without the need for explicit rule-based reasoning.
The scene graph model is first optimized for clarity and efficiency, and then a traffic scene generation model is developed to explicitly capture the elements of a environment that are missing in graph representations, specifically human behavior and physical forces.
We validate SceneGen's effectiveness in providing realistic traffic scenarios for actual self-driving cars, demonstrating superior performance over existing scene graph models and demonstrating the limitations of using simplified approaches to model the environment.
When using generated scenarios for training self-driving vehicles, our approach results in significantly reduced accidents compared to existing methods, highlighting its superior performance in creating a more accurate traffic environment.
On a Cayley tree, we analyze the Ising model and find novel periodic measures that are linked to index-2 normal subgroups within its group representation.

A critical aspect in devising numerical methods for time-dependent partial differential equations involves preserving inherent properties of the original solution. Researchers have a rich history of developing and analyzing preservation-based discretization techniques, including the Lie derivative, the Hamiltonian, and the finite-element methods. When paired with appropriate time integration techniques, these methods can produce numerical solutions that faithfully mirror key features of the original system. However, due to the increasing size and complexity of the algebraic systems generated by this approach, their direct solution often proves to be computationally expensive. In order to overcome this limitation, researchers have turned to iterative solvers, such as the conjugate gradient method. In order to enhance the efficiency of these iterative solutions, preconditioners have been proposed that retain the geometric properties of the original discretization. This proposal includes a range of candidates for preconditioning techniques, spanning from novel to well-established methods. By providing a comprehensive framework for evaluating and comparing these preconditioning strategies, the proposed method includes a standardized testbed consisting of two prominent models, namely the harmonic oscillator and the pendulum equation.

A group of integer sequences can be considered jointly ergodic if for any ergodic system with a measure preservation characteristic, the average value of their simultaneous occurrences converges to the product of their individual occurrences as the evaluation scale grows infinitely. This definition builds on the existing understanding of individual ergodicity. This work expands on previous research by completing key ergodic-theory applications previously only partially demonstrated in the literature, utilizing these extensions to prove the independence of certain sequence sequences through the Fundamental Theorem. Specifically, the independence of Rogers' sequences was confirmed using this approach.

We investigated the effects of dust grain growth on the formation process in low-metallicity environments, resembling early galaxies, through massive supernovae simulations. Using the simulation, we were able to track the evolution of dust grains from initial formation to grain growth and reprocessing of light by these growing dusts. The simulation accounted for the radiation transfer, chemical reactions, and dynamics in a molecular cloud core with a mass of 0.37 solar masses and a temperature of 10 Kelvin. The cloud, surrounding a supernova with 11.87 solar masses, had low metallicity and experienced grain growth due to the accumulation of iron group elements and silicon on dust particles. This led to an increase in dust size from 10^-6 cm to 10^-4 cm within 300 days, which in turn altered the dust opacity and heating rate, ultimately affecting the cloud's collapse and potential star formation process.

Detecting objects at a far distance in three dimensions is crucial for real-world applications like urban driving. Current methods for 3D object detection, whether based on LiDAR or image-based, struggle with detecting objects far away. The primary challenge in LiDAR-based methods lies in accurately estimating the location and orientation of distant objects, as the effective field of view is significantly limited. On the other hand, image-based approaches find it difficult to resolve objects at a far range due to the significant information loss in images. To address this issue, the Image + LiDAR approach fuses both perspectives but suffers from the sparse nature of LiDAR data, which creates large holes. Building on these difficulties, the authors introduce the concept of Far-Field 3D Detection (Far3Det), which aims to achieve the accurate 3D localization of objects at a far distance, using a single LiDAR sensor. They design the Semi-Dense 3D Anchor Box Regression (Sd3AaR) module to densely predict 3D bounding boxes for objects in the far distance, effectively mitigating the sparsity of LiDAR data. The proposed method demonstrates superior performance in detecting objects at a far range, outperforming state-of-the-art LiDAR-based and Image-based approaches on the nuScenes validation set.

Chemical reactions can be comprehensively understood through the identification of ground states and transition states within a potential energy landscape, which is mapped out by the cost function of a variational wavefunction. However, this approach faces significant computational challenges due to the high dimensionality of the problem. To circumvent this, we present a quantum machine learning framework that generates approximate ground states for a reduced set of nuclear configurations, thereby decreasing the problem's complexity to a more manageable size. This framework is further enhanced by employing reinforcement learning to optimize the parameterization of the variational wavefunction. Initially, we evaluate our approach for hydrogen molecules and subsequently, we investigate its potential for use in calculating ground states for more complex systems, such as water molecules.

Soft-tissue navigation is highly dependent on non-rigid registration, which can be optimized by leveraging virtual endoscopy technology. To achieve accurate non-rigid registration, a model based on the physical properties of the tissue must first be created. This study proposes a novel approach that utilizes a computationally efficient, finite-element method to simulate a biomechanical model of the organ, which is driven by local forces determined through a probabilistic method. The model is further refined by incorporating a compact representation of the mechanical model, thus enabling real-time volume-to-surface registration. Notably, the proposed approach is among the first to integrate a biomechanical model with a probabilistic inference framework suitable for soft-tissue applications, which has been demonstrated through simulations and experimental trials using phantoms and in vivo data, yielding promising results.

For a static, spherically symmetric spacetime, research has focused on conformal matter collineations within the energy-momentum tensor. The overall structure of these collineations is determined under non-degenerate conditions, with fifteen distinct, independent forms found. However, when the energy-momentum tensor becomes degenerate, the associated conformal collineations exhibit infinite degrees of freedom. Moreover, specific degenerate subcases may still harbor non-degenerate Ricci inheritance collineations.

Determining scene flow involves calculating the three-dimensional motion trajectories of objects within an environment, which is a critical process with wide-ranging applications in robotics and the automotive industry. This task is particularly complex due to its 3D nature and the presence of unknown parameters. Researchers have developed effective strategies to address these challenges by utilizing pairs of consecutive images, but these approaches still face challenges in handling ambiguous regions and ensuring robustness against variations in lighting and weather conditions. To overcome these challenges, researchers have turned to self-supervised learning techniques, which allow models to be trained without the need for manual annotation. They have also explored the use of self-supervised metric learning to represent each scene flow estimation problem within a unique, distance-based embedding space. However, they discovered that the features learned through conventional 2D image regression methods already contain sufficient information to distinguish between different scene flow estimations, which confuses the metric learning component and leads to degraded performance. To investigate this issue further, they conducted controlled experiments and discovered that models trained through self-supervised image regression techniques are particularly vulnerable to adversarial perturbations, which in turn causes the embedding space to become distorted. They hypothesized that this vulnerability is at the root of the poor performance observed in end-to-end self-supervised scene flow estimation models. To validate this, they introduced a novel adversarial metric learning objective to intentionally train the model with adversarial inputs, which allowed them to introduce a significant performance boost of over 10% in Conda and

In recent years, AI networks, specifically those based on artificial neural systems, have significantly outperformed competitors in a wide range of tasks including image recognition, sound analysis, and language interpretation. However, widespread use of such models was hindered until now by their substantial computational demands and high energy consumption during operation. Neural engineering models, in particular memristive and spike-based neural networks, have shown great potential for efficient processing on neuro-synaptic chips, particularly in classifying patterns. Despite initial successes in integrating these models with other technologies like random forests, there were limitations, such as the need to artificially train the networks before use. This study presents a novel approach that combines spiking random neural networks with random forest ensembles to accurately classify patterns like MNIST and EMNIST, using only raw data and benefiting from both SRRNN feature extraction and random forest classification capabilities.

This research investigates the thermodynamic characteristics of spin-polarized strange quark matter under a strong magnetic field at finite temperature, applying the MIT bag model. Furthermore, we derived the equation of state for spin-polarized strange quark matter in the presence of a strong magnetic field, and subsequently, we examined the structure of spin-polarized strange quark stars across varying temperatures and magnetic fields.

A Perfect-Matching-Hamiltonian property in a graph implies that each perfect matching can be combined with another to create a Hamiltonian cycle. This concept was first introduced by Las Vergnas in 1979 and further explored by Thomassen in 1994, who identified a set of 14 cubic bipartite graphs with 36 edges where the property holds, notably including the 12-edge-3-vertex graph represented as K_{3,3} K_{2}. A graph is considered to have the PMH-property if it is bipartite and exhibits the Perfect-Matching-Hamiltonian characteristic. The edge-colouring vector of a graph consists of the frequencies of colour pairs that form perfect matchings within its different edge-colourings. This study introduces a subset of the edge-transitive graphs, specifically those with a prime number of colours, where the graph is limited to having edge-colouring vectors that include only the edge-transitive graph. We introduce the ETP-hamiltonian characteristic, define graphs with this characteristic as ETP-hamiltonian, and prove that if an edge-transitive graph with the Perfect-Matching-Hamiltonian property also has the edge-transitive graph, then it is Hamiltonian.
