A major challenge in creating AI systems that can automatically process and analyze historical documents is accurately training models to visually recognize and extract information from these documents. Our proposed solution, called Voucher2Voucher (V2V), is a training dataset and model framework that can trained models to visually extract information from a variety of document types. Unlike traditional methods that require training models visually on every document type separately, V2V allows for a single-model approach that works on multiple document types. The V2V dataset is a comprehensive collection of over 100,000 documents across 13 categories, spanning from bank statements to utility bills. The V2V model is a single-model approach that was visually trained using only the Voucher2Voucher dataset. The model was then tested on a variety of documents, achieving satisfactory results in extracting over 90% of key fields accurately. Furthermore, the success of V2V demonstrates the potential for using visually rich documents as the primary source of training data for models that process visually complex documents, and significantly reduces the computational costs associated with developing such models.

The collaboration between the Laser Interferometer Gravitational-Wave Observatory and other institutions detects mergers of compact objects that produce gravitational waves. These detections offer insights into the population of these objects and help resolve astrophysical questions. However, the parameter estimation and identification of specific features, such as the masses of the objects involved, can be complicated and time-consuming through conventional methods. Machine learning techniques offer an alternative, enabling rapid processing of large amounts of data, which has already been successfully applied to the analysis of binary black hole and binary neutron star mergers. This work aims to evaluate the performance of deep learning methods in detecting and extracting specific information from neutron star-neutron star mergers. The results indicate that these methods can achieve satisfactory outcomes in certain scenarios but struggle in others, particularly in identifying the nature of the objects involved. Furthermore, the study found that deep learning methods can identify events with a degree of confidence exceeding 99%, whereas conventional methods can do so with over 99.9% certainty. This discrepancy has significant implications for scientific conclusions and future research in this field.

The adverse effects of social determinants of health on the quality of care and healthcare disparities have been well-documented. Building electronic health records to capture social determinants of health is being advocated to address this issue. However, the labor-intensive process of manually annotating data has limited their application. This study explores the development of a novel multi-task learning framework, called M²NEU, for training neural network systems to extract social determinants of health data from health care claims. Using three distinct neural network sub-systems, M²NEU effectively learned to identify and extract relevant data, outperforming existing methods on benchmark datasets for homelessness detection, food insecurity, and housing instability.

This study is centered on a two-part swimmer known as the scallop, which transitions through varying dynamics across two different fluid environments. We resolve two optimal control scenarios, one focused on achieving the fastest time to relocate the swimmer and another on finding the most energy-efficient method using periodic control to move it between predetermined positions. Leveraging the simplicity provided by limiting switching to one point and taking advantage of the underlying equation's structure, we can identify all possible responses to the swimmer's movement and evaluate the efficiency of varying strategies. We also provide a method to determine the starting conditions that lead to a specific one-point switch and demonstrate how the starting conditions can be completely determined with a single-point switch or at least two gamma variations in the absence of switches. We also explore the efficiency of the swimmer's motion and successfully design a method to find optimal starting conditions for a specific one-point switch in a model featuring two channels with distinct flow characteristics.

Urban settings are known to be socially and economically diverse and have a positive societal effect. During the pandemic, lockdown measures limited urban diversity of social interactions. This study analyzes how COVID-19 affected city goers' mobility patterns in 2020 in comparison to 2019 in six US cities. It also examines the impact on the economic diversity of those interactions. Findings show that mobility in 2019 generally followed a bimodal distribution, with 70% of locations exhibiting higher economic diversity. However, during the pandemic, mobility decreased by 30% and economic diversity dropped to 50%. On average, visiting a city resulted in encounters with 3.5 times more economically diverse individuals post-pandemic. Government-mandated restrictions altered mobility, with locations previously visited less during weekdays now seeing increased visits. This change boosted weekend and overall average economic diversity. Furthermore, the study discovered that different locations in the same city varied greatly in their pandemic impacts. In some areas, economic diversity dropped to 90%, while in others it only decreased by 10%. These areas differed in pre-pandemic mobility, with lower-traffic areas experiencing greater diversity losses.

Three-dimensional simulations of young stellar objects were conducted for various mass outcomes, ranging from less than 1 solar mass to as much as 100 solar masses. The simulations used existing initial conditions and were observed for up to 100,000 seconds. It was found that large inflows, often accompanied by gas density enhancements and velocity increases of one to two kilometers per second, were observed in all mass scenarios. The frequency and intensity of these episodic accretion events varied with mass, with lower mass scenarios experiencing more events of intermediate intensity, and higher mass scenarios experiencing more events of greater intensity. These events were found to be caused by changes in the disk's outer edge, often involving spiral arms and jets. Jet activity was observed in all mass scenarios in the early stages but was observed in fewer than half of the simulations after 10 solar masses. It was also observed that binary interactions led to increased mixing of gas and contributed to further mixing of gas in binary systems.

Building upon the mass-gap property, we construct a realisation of wedge-localised observables from a given Poincaré invariant net of observables in two-dimensional QFT using endomorphisms defined by Longo-Witten. This realisation maintains unitary equivalence to the original net while exhibiting wedge locality. Furthermore, we demonstrate that the S-matrix derived from this construction is non-trivial for chiral CFT with central charge greater than zero.

Implementing 5G cellular base stations in highly populated and developed areas is being accelerated, which has 3GPP-defined Specific Absorption Rate (SAR) limits that govern the maximum exposure of children and other people to these facilities. To assess the actual experience children and others have with 5G base stations in various environments, including children's vehicles, schools, and hospitals, this study uses measured data from multiple sources, including 25G cars, to evaluate the maximum exposure in accordance with SAR standards. The analysis covers all possible 5G frequency bands used globally, and the results are presented in tables and charts for various scenarios, including children's vehicles, roads, schools, hospitals, and 5G tower proximity when people are inside buildings. Notably, in this study's measured maximum exposure scenarios, users are exposed to up to 40 times less than the SAR-limited exposure in accordance with the 25G standards.

This research examines a specific scenario where the average vorticity fluctuates,
utilizing a closed form representation of the water's flow in terms of its surface movements.
Instead of linearizing the governing equations, we analyze waves with fluctuating vorticity.
Our findings show that for situations with higher wave amplitudes, a specific equation
accurately represents the dynamics of the system over extended periods, accurately
replicating Dysthe's wave model with fluctuating vorticity.
Furthermore, for situations with lower wave amplitudes, our proposed equation
produces results that closely align with those of fully numerically simulated wave events.

In this proof, a modified Stokes formula for differential forms is demonstrated on the space of locally convex differential forms of compact support. Additionally, this demonstration includes an analog of the Stokes formula for Borel measures, using form-bidual differential forms.

Autonomous navigation in diverse and ever-changing environments demands self-propelled vehicles to quickly identify and avoid obstacles within their surroundings. In dynamic indoor settings, our team presents a novel, sonar-based navigation framework for a mobile robot named NaviOne. This system integrates a hierarchical control scheme with forward, distance, and bearing controllers, and features a innovative, real-time 2D environmental mapping method that maps objects and surfaces using a composite format. By employing an efficient, differential-drive kinematic model, the robot can interpret and utilize sonar data for seamless navigation. NaviOne's integration of hardware, software, and a sophisticated control system enables enhanced navigation capabilities in complex indoor spaces. In contrast to existing navigation systems that rely on laser range finders, our approach excels in detecting objects at close range and operates effectively with fewer sensors. In contrast to existing indoor navigation systems that utilize 2D laser scanners, our system achieves comparable performance with only 12 sonar sensors.

The prevalence of false news on social media poses a significant threat of spreading panic and misinformation. Research has shown that language patterns can help distinguish between genuine and fabricated news articles. This study explores the potential of using pre-trained classifiers, such as BERT, to identify the authenticity of news based on both the linguistic styles inherent to false or real information and the inherent potential of their intrinsic structures. A key challenge in this research is that many sums of complex news sources result in summaries that are difficult for classifiers to process effectively. To tackle this issue, various preprocessing methods were applied to both raw data and generated summaries. The outcomes of this study show that combining the use of BERT and a specific class of transformers, namely RoBERTa, can accurately classify false and real news based on their respective data patterns. A comprehensive analysis of the results is provided to support this conclusion.

This research investigates complex systems that follow stochastic patterns by using mathematical structures known as random field models. The study focuses on analyzing a specific aspect of these systems – the geometry of their parametric space – using statistical tools to simulate and model the systems' dynamics. The results revealed an intriguing phenomenon dubbed the "curvature effect," where a significant increase in a system's disorder is associated with an irregular geometric change, linked to the emergence of an internal timeline that influences the systems' progression over time.

This research targets resolving secrecy concerns for nonorthogonal multiple access users by introducing an alternative decoding order method. First, we mathematically quantify the total possible decoding order options. We then propose an effective decoding order approach that guarantees positive secrecy rates for each user and, through computation, determine the feasible secure decoding order quantities. To minimize complexity in determining the best secure decoding order, we also present an efficient yet suboptimal solution strategy. Notably, the proposed suboptimal solution achieves around 137% improvement in performance over a relevant benchmark solution.

When applying dimensionality reduction techniques to datasets with anomalies, L1-PCA has been a widely used non-Gaussian method. This study focuses on a variation of rotationally invariant IPCA, proposing an iterative algorithm to solve it using the proximal alternating linearized minimization approach. The convergence of a local optimum is proven for specific conditions, highlighting the importance of initial settings and sample size. Furthermore, the theoretical framework is simplified to include cases of rotational invariance and bias. This includes exploring the impact of data skewness on convergence rates and the influence of anomalies on optimal solutions, particularly in scenarios of significant variance.

Traditionally, annotated data has served as a guiding reference for machine learning models to replicate human labeling and generate corresponding emotional labels. However, the reliance on pre-existing annotated datasets no longer serves as a natural evaluation platform for semantic labeling methods, given that both are assessed against human-generated emotion labels. To circumvent this limitation, a novel framework is proposed which takes a different approach: it generates semantic labels for Wikipedia articles and evaluates their alignment with human emotion labels. Specifically, the proposed AEC-BERT method, which integrates the WikiQA dataset, produces emotional labels that correspond to the human emotion labels. Meanwhile, utterances from the Wikipedia pages are utilized to generate semantic annotations that match the human emotion labels. Experimental evidence shows that AEC-BERT outperforms existing labeling methods including BERT+CRF, BERT+SVM, BERT+LR, and BERT+MLP in accordance with emotion-related queries. Furthermore, the assessment results verify that the semantic labels produced by BEC-BERT excel in quality compared to other methods including BERT+CRF, BERT+SVM, BERT+LR, BERT+MLP.

Kopczyński and Waśkiewski extended traditional finite energy games to include ordered sets with a torus structure in 2013. In this work, we expand that concept to include totally ordered groups, particularly those based on exponential scales like $\mathbb{Z}[\mathbb{X}]$. We demonstrate that strategy existence for these extended games can still be achieved using a variant of the Banach-Mazur game, using $\mathbb{X}$-countable partial cuts of the order type $\mathbb{X}$.

The subclass of magnetic Cataclysmic Variables, asynchronous polars, still lacks a comprehensive understanding. Asynchronous polars are a category of polars characterized by their white dwarf spin period differing significantly, whether longer or shorter, from their binary orbital period. The detection rate of asynchronous polars in soft gamma-ray observations is disproportionately high compared to their overall population prevalence, hinting at possible distinct properties when contrasted with standard high-state accretion flow-powered polars. To explore the unique features of asynchronous polars, we conducted a detailed analysis of standard polar systems, specifically matching asynchronous ones, using data from Chandra observations during their typical states. The sample size for this comparison is 14, consisting of 8 asynchronous and 6 synchronous polars. In contrast to non-synchronous polars, standard synchronous polars display similar average values for X-ray flux, 0.6 keV absorption, and spectral slope. There appears to be a notable discrepancy between the average X-ray flux values (at the 2.5 sigma confidence level) and absorption values (at the 2 sigma confidence level) between asynchronous and synchronous polars, with the former exhibiting lower values in both instances. However, it's important to note that due to the limited sample size, further data collection is necessary to confirm these findings with greater certainty.

This project's primary goal is to investigate the integration of the Reduced Basis Method (RBM) with distinct Fluid-Structure Interaction (FSI) approaches, namely a monolithic method and a partitioned technique. We will detail the implementation of two reduction methods and then apply them to a common test case, with a focus on a monolithic approach, solving both fluid and solid problems simultaneously, and a partitioned approach, solving these problems separately with a fixed point strategy. To evaluate these methods, we'll use a variant of the Turek-Hron benchmark test case, characterized by a fluid Reynolds number of 100.

For mobile robots to successfully navigate unfamiliar surroundings independently, having an effective mapping and navigation system is crucial. Current research has produced various state-of-the-art methods for creating map representations, yet most of these methods are complex and provide a comprehensive overview, making further development challenging. In response to this, a novel, modular framework called HiTMap is presented. This allows for easy expansion with different features and mapping modules, providing a unique advantage. Furthermore, a new representation called a hierarchical topological map is presented, utilizing points of interest to effectively summarize the layout of an environment, thereby significantly decreasing data storage requirements. Experimental results on both simulated and real-world environments demonstrate that HiTMap enables a mobile robot to navigate with relative ease, exhibiting robust performance even when encountering significant disturbances, while maintaining competitive accuracy compared to leading methods.

The UM-IU@LING system for the 2019 SemEval OffensEval Task is the subject of this paper. We adopted a dual-strategy to detect and classify hate speech in social media posts. For subtask A, a BERT-based classifier was adapted and achieved a high macro F1 score of 0.8286 in evaluating test data, thereby ranking 3rd among 103 competitors. Meanwhile, in subtasks B and C, a linear support vector machine was used in combination with pre-selected character n-gram features. Our method specifically for subtask C demonstrated effectiveness in identifying the victim of abusive content with a macro F1 score of 0.5553, and ranked 25th out of 65 participants.

One of the key challenges in metrology lies in the metrology triangle, a problem that arises from the difficulty of cross-checking fundamental constants with the same precision as required. To address this challenge, a new method has been proposed, involving a combination of atomic interferometry and magnetic interferometry to measure the fine structure constant with a new, more efficient approach. This method takes advantage of atomic interference and the Meissner effect to enhance the impact of a local magnetic field, making it more sensitive. By leveraging the amplification provided by atomic interference and the Meissner effect, the proposed method can achieve a significant increase in precision, contributing to a deeper understanding of atomic physics and the basic principles that underlie these phenomena. This research has the potential to contribute to the development of future methods for cross-checking atomic and electronic standards of resistance and fine structure constant with a high degree of precision. Although a prototype has so far shown a factor of 10^5 improvement in sensitivity over conventional atomic interferometry, there is room for further improvement, and the precision may reach the level of atomic physics experiments that challenge the standard model of atomic physics.

We investigate the emergence of magnetocaloric effect (MCE) in two-dimensional transition metal dichalcogenides due to their proximity with a ferromagnetic substrate, specifically a MoTe$_2$ monolayer on EuO with a heat source. Using a tight-binding model that incorporates proximity-induced exchange and Rashba fields, we analyze how these exotic phenomena arise under varying parameters including Rashba and exchange field strengths, as well as Fermi energy and heat source intensity. Our study reveals the capability to induce MCE in MoTe$_2$ and demonstrates its light source potential. Moreover, we find that the MCE in MoTe$_2$ surpasses that in EuO, along with the opportunity to tailor this effect through the adjustment of proximal ferromagnetic properties, Rashba spin splitting, and external electric fields. These findings highlight the significant opportunity to leverage MCE in MoTe$_2$ for magnetic field-free cooling applications in spintronics.

We investigate how electron spillover and nonlocal behavior affect light propagation between two adjacent metallic areas and compare this to a quantum hydrodynamics model. We demonstrate that a quantum hydrodynamics model which incorporates both phenomena yields accurate results, particularly as the gap narrows, in contrast to a local response model which generates unphysical results such as spontaneous spillover kinetic energy and altered frequency behavior. Notably, the hydrodynamics model which accounts for both effects is equivalent to a Hermitian tight-binding model with dipole-dipole interactions which allows us to describe the transition from gap to no-gap and the resulting dynamics.

The Calculus of Constructions, introduced in 1985 by Coquand, has been a driving force in the development of dependent type theories since its inception. In 2009, Simon Castellan achieved the first constructive proof of its strong normalization using a normalization-by-editing approach, building on Annenkov's work from 2006. Although this proof was significant, its complexity made understanding and further development challenging due to multiple layers of transformation introduced. In 2012, Schellinx and van der Weide presented a simplified understanding of the CaC's structure, which has since facilitated the creation of alternative, more accessible proofs for its consistency, including a proof based on the logical relations method. The focus of this article is on the Calculus of Constructions and its key extensions, including Inductive-Recursive Definitions, Large Eliminations, and Universes.

We invite undergraduate students and early graduate students to an educational introduction to one-dimensional topological phases, focusing on the Su-Schrieffer-Heeger model. This will include discussions on entanglement using the correlator method and von Neumann density matrix, as well as geometric phase, polarization, and transport characteristics, all with consideration of electron-electron interactions and periodic driving forces. Several available codes for these numerical methods are examined, and we hope to encourage the development of similar tools targeted at educational purposes.

In the case of a finite admixture model whose components and weights are unknown, techniques from stochastic convex geometry help us determine how the number of identifiable components changes in response to an increase in the amount of collected data. Additionally, placing a Dirichlet process prior on densities within a defined range enables us to recover a measure that narrows to the specific identifiable components, thereby yielding the corresponding admixture weights. A new algorithm is then proposed to accurately capture the complexity of data by utilizing only the minimum number of components necessary.

We derive the two-loop AdS$_5$ vacuum energy with four gravitons at the peak of its interaction depth using the conformal field theory, 
demonstrating that perturbative finiteness is contingent upon the cancellation of specific logarithmic and constant terms in the amplitude. 
The cancellation of the logarithmic terms is found to be inherent to the structure of the amplitude, 
whereas the constancy requires a precise computation. 
This calculation yields a specific value for the constant, 
demonstrating that it is not accounted for by the contributions of witten diagrams in the conformal field theory. 
The presence of finite contributions not explained by the witten diagrams indicates the existence of quantum corrections to the AdS$_5$ vacuum energy. 
This finding signifies that the graviton remains unitary at the two-loop level.

High-performance computing on SIMD devices, including GPUs, has historically been challenging for object-oriented programming due to inefficiencies in memory allocation and access.  Despite this limitation, a range of applications, including real-world programs with inherent object structures, have been excluded from leveraging the vast computing power now available on GPU clusters.  To address this barrier, we developed DynaSOAr, a high-level parallel memory allocator that enables efficient use of shared memory for single- and multi-object operations.  By extending the C++ standard template library, DynaSOAr provides a rich set of data structure constructs and optimizes memory access through a vectorized approach and advanced caching mechanisms.  Our solution specifically targets the limitations of GPU architecture, which, although it features a high-bandwidth memory, is hindered by its lack of virtual address space and inefficient context switching.  With DynaSOAr, we can now run high-level object operations in shared memory, significantly enhancing the feasibility of GPU cluster-based HP/cap computing for object-oriented programming.  Our system has been demonstrated to efficiently allocate up to 1TB of NVIDIA V100 memory across 4 GPUs, while delivering near-optimal performance in shared memory operations.  Furthermore, we have developed three context-specific extensions to further expand its capabilities, which have been showcased through custom applications, including a dynaSOAr-based implementation of the context switch problem that outperforms its CPU-based counterpart by a factor of 87 in runtime. This paper investigates the boundedness of a diverse set of operators, including those generated by the Calderón-Zygmund operators and the fractional integral operator, on generalized mixed Morrey spaces. Additionally, the article examines the boundedness of the commutators of these operators on the same space. Furthermore, specific applications are considered to obtain the boundedness of several operators, such as the Hardy-Littlewood maximal operator and the Calderón-Zygmund singular integral operators, on generalized mixed Morrey spaces.

A comprehensive theoretical framework is developed to predict the spectral characteristics of magnetic impurities or small clusters located on the surface of a superconductor. The model is based on density functional theory and includes full relativistic effects. The application of this model to a single Mn atom and a dimer on the Nb(110) superconducting surface demonstrates the capability of the approach. Full spectral resolution is achieved with the inclusion of a non-perturbative electron electron correlation solver and the electron-phonon coupling. The impact of the Kohn-Sham spectrum and the Crystal-moment on the state width is also examined.

Our proposal, FourierMask, integrates the Fourier series with implicit neural networks to create instance segmentation masks. FourierMask uses a Fourier transformation on the coordinate positions and feeds the mapped features to an implicit function for pixel value prediction. As a result, the function outputs a mask without the need for explicit grid-based predictions. Since implicit functions can extrapolate beyond their training range, FourierMask can predict masks for instances beyond their visible boundaries using only a descriptive input, such as an ID or bounding box. This capability allows it to excel in tasks like referring expression generation and image captioning. Furthermore, FourierMask shows promising results in sub-task performance, including precision-recall curves, R@K scores, and other evaluation metrics.

This study examines how the discrete nature of the frequency spectrum for a non-compact manifold embedded in a higher-dimensional space affects its boundary points, focusing particularly on the Hausdorff dimension of those boundary points. Specifically, if a flat, extrinsically bounded two-dimensional surface is mapped onto a bounded, three-dimensional convex area, and the boundary points have a certain measure, the surface will have a discrete frequency spectrum. The theorem is relevant to recent research involving the construction of bounded, flat disks, and it answers a previously asked question about the frequency spectrum of certain surfaces. Additionally, this study demonstrates the precision of its results by showing counter-examples and a new method for identifying essential frequencies.

Current retrievals of cloud optical thickness and particle size using passive satellite imaging techniques fail for optically dense convective clouds. These clouds contain a shadowed central region with altered properties compared to the clouds' outer edges. This study introduces the concept of a cloudy core to explain this phenomenon. Using data from the MISR and MODIS satellite imagers, we found that the veiled core of highly opaque clouds often matches or even exceeds the cloud's optical thickness in size. Additionally, the core typically exhibits a larger particle size than the surrounding clouds, a size that is often accessible to satellite imaging techniques. This discovery has significant implications for understanding and modeling the physical and chemical processes occurring within clouds.

We examined how a laser pulse with a changing frequency impacts its passage through a sub-wavelength target and the acceleration of ions. Our investigation focused on a laser pulse with frequency variations, and we observed that a certain level of asymmetry in the pulse can trigger a rapid increase in energy within a few picoseconds. When this level of energy is sufficiently high, it can accelerate protons to a significant energy level of 150 MeV. As a result, it is essential to consider the presence of a certain level of frequency variation in the pulse to effectively utilize a tiny target for achieving high energy proton acceleration.

The space telescope TESS has opened up a vast exploration area for researchers, allowing for a wide range of stellar studies. In response to this, numerous candidate systems have been identified that warrant closer examination with the help of ground-based telescopes utilizing high-precision methods. One such system is TOI-712, a system hosting three transiting mini-Neptunes with a period spanning from 10 to 20 Earth days. Through a combination of transit, radial velocity, and transit photometry techniques, we have established a comprehensive understanding of the TOI-712 system. TOI-712 A, the primary star, is a K-type star in the subgiant phase, characterized by a mass of 0.81 solar masses, a radius of 2.35 solar radii, and a relatively short age of 2.3 billion years. In contrast, TOI-712 B, the companion star, is an M-type dwarf in the main sequence phase, classified as 0.39 solar masses, 0.40 solar radii, and shares the same age as the system. Although TOI-712 lacks a habitable zone, the TOI-712 A system has the potential for a fourth planet with 60% probability, with a 15 Earth-day orbit.

We investigated the electronic and magnetic properties of carbon and nitrogen defects within TiO2 rutile using the PBE0 hybrid DFT method, with results compared to experimental data and those from the PBE method. Our study considered the implications of using approximate (PBE) vs. accurate (PBE0) exchange for identifying the correct ground and excited states within this system. Key findings include: (a) carbon nitrogen defects exhibit similar overall behavior to oxygen vacancies in terms of stability, (b) carbon defects with sp^2 and sp^3 configurations follow similar trends in total energy as seen in experiments, and (c) calculations reveal the possibility of antiferromagnetic stability in certain configurations of carbon doped TiO2.

This letter describes the inspiration and an analytical method for detecting the production of top-quark pairs in the Large Hadron Collider through the identification of protons emitted at the front end. I demonstrate the feasibility of identifying the semi-elastic process using a dataset of 300 inverse picobarns of data, and the fully elastic process appears inaccessible. Furthermore, I illustrate that utilizing forward proton tags enables limits on certain rare top-quark decays such as $t\rightarrow u\gamma$ and $t\rightarrow c\gamma$ which would significantly surpass the current world records, with limits on branching ratios of $<0.39\times10^{-5}$ and $<0.99\times10^{-5}$ respectively.

Observations of the intra-cluster medium with X-rays are of great assistance in understanding the physics of galaxy clusters. However, current X-ray imaging and spectroscopy can only provide a limited number of measurements of emission properties, which are averaged out over arcs of sight. As next-generation X-ray telescopes are set to be launched, precise mapping of the intra-cluster medium will become possible, where line-of-sight quantities will be derived to identify statistical patterns in the data. Before doing so, a key factor needs to be established: the uncertainty in the estimation of structure functions derived from such data sets. This study presents the calculation of the uncertainty in the first and second-order structure functions, accounting for the non-Gaussian nature of counting statistics, and determines the influence of various parameters on the uncertainty of these functions, including the data normalization, the size of the lag, the number of realizations, and the redshift distribution of the involved galaxy clusters. Notably, it is determined that the normalization of the counts per pixel has the most notable effect on the uncertainty of the structure functions. Additionally, the study demonstrates that the uncertainty in the second-order structure functions may be used to identify the presence of shock fronts in the intra-cluster medium.

In 1993, Erdos and Galvin pioneered upper density problems within Ramsey theory, specifically the problem of identifying the highest $\lambda$ Ramsey $k$-colorable edge-factored complete graph $K_{n(n)}$ in an infinitely divided graph that contains all color patterns. We expand upon this research by investigating whether the concept of upper density varies with different graph factors, particularly those that include cliques of different sizes and colors. We provide a method to relate the upper density of any two graph factors, thereby providing upper density estimates for several notable edge-factors, including uniquely factorable graphs, cycle-factors, complete bipartite graphs, and complete multigraphs. Additionally, we introduce a general framework to obtain upper density inequalities in a broader context and introduce the associated concept of Ramsey chromatic number with upper density.

Located at the heart of the Milky Way lies the Central Molecular Zone (CMZ), a distinct ring-like formation, where analysis of the 230 GHz $^{13}$CO isotopologue spectrum from the PEPPIN survey has been conducted. Utilizing spectral fitting with COLDENSO, the gas density structure within the CMZ has been measured. Further analysis using 2D correlation functions using 2D ellipse fits has been performed. It was discovered that the gas density within the CMZ exhibits a pronounced anisotropic two-component structure, with major and minor axes correlated lengths of 210 pc and 100 pc, respectively. Notably, the gas density within the CMZ is higher along the major axis by a factor of 1.5 to 2. These findings suggest that the gas within the CMZ is not randomly distributed but rather anisotropically an elongated gas structure likely influenced by a combination of gravitational forces and magnetic fields.

This paper introduces a groundbreaking method for identifying Bell's Palsy solely by analyzing a person's eye movements in a video. We have devised a unique approach that relies on extracting features from the visible blood vessels in the eye, which we call EIA-Net. Our method stands out as the first of its kind to detect Bell's Palsy using only video, without the need for other assessments. Our experiments have demonstrated superior results when compared to existing methods for eye examination, with notably lower error rates in identifying the condition. We believe our eye-centric approach can significantly aid medical professionals in providing prompt and reliable diagnoses of Bell's Palsy patients.

Our analysis highlights the benefits of using qudits instead of qubits in scalar Quantum Electrodynamics in $(1+1)$d, specifically regarding their tolerance to errors. When measuring the mass gap using an out-of-time correlator as noise increases from both amplitude damping and Pauli channels, our findings show that simulations utilizing qutrits can handle up to 10 to 100 times more gate noise than their qubit-based counterparts for the same mass determination error. Furthermore, while achieving a 20 percent accuracy for the mass gap may become achievable with state-of-the-art quantum processors in the near future using a tQED model, our results suggest that employing qutrits could potentially achieve the same result with significantly less introduced gate noise.

Research indicates that positrons are efficiently produced through interactions between intense lasers and solid materials, specifically within the context of strong-field quantum electrodynamics. However, the polarization properties of these positrons remain unexplored. Our study utilizes particle-in-cell simulations with full quantum effects to analyze the polarization characteristics of positrons generated from high-density, multi-planned foil targets illuminated by intense lasers. The results reveal that the generated positrons possess significant polarization levels, exceeding 10%, and this level of polarization can be enhanced by increasing the thickness of the foil. Furthermore, the polarization properties of these positrons are highly sensitive to the orientation of the laser's electric field relative to the foil's normal axis, with the maximum levels of polarization observed when these axes are aligned. This research opens up exciting possibilities for the development of polarized positron sources and potential applications in fields such as polarized $e^+e^-$ colliders and studies involving positron scattering and scattering of positron beams.

Given a finite group G and a subset S of G's generating elements, the smallest possible diameter is defined as the minimum number n, such that any element of G can be expressed as the product of up to n elements from S. This research focuses on characterizing groups with a diameter that scales polynomially for a fixed-sized generating set, and it demonstrates that these groups have a significant abelian subgroup close to the order of the group itself. This finding reinforces an important conjecture by Brodsky and Kurland and builds upon existing results, and it also establishes upper and lower bounds related to the growth rate of certain groups, and it is shown that some of these bounds are close in value, and it is demonstrated that a major part of the upper bound can be removed with only a slight increase in the polynomial's degree, and it is shown that the underlying mechanism of the argument reveals the critical feature of groups with a polynomial diameter, and it demonstrates that these groups have a significant solvable subgroup that accounts for a major portion of the group order, and it is shown that this finding supports an important result by Pyber and Szab\'o, and it demonstrates that the underlying mechanism of the argument reveals the critical feature of groups with a polynomial diameter, and it shows that these groups have a significant nilpotent subgroup that accounts for a major portion of the group order, and it demonstrates that this finding supports an important result by Pyber and Szab\'o, and it shows that

This research develops a fully integrated CMOS temperature sensor that is capable of measuring and providing both maximum and minimum temperatures. The temperature sensor is designed with a wide operating voltage range and incorporates a novel architecture based on a ring oscillator and bandgap circuits. It is capable of converting, storing, and comparing temperatures with an extremely low energy consumption. The proposed circuit is compatible with a 0.6V - 1.8V supply voltage and operates at room temperature. The temperature resolution is 0.24°C, and the inaccuracy is 1.4°C for minimum/maximum temperature. The maximum and minimum temperatures are -40.45°C and 84.92°C, and -40.45°C and 85.08°C, respectively. The current consumption is 15.5nA and 12.5nA for minimum/maximum temperature. The energy per conversion is 1.06pJ at 0.6V and 35us.

Long-lasting stability in the magnetic fields of Ap stars, white dwarfs, and neutron stars has been observed despite the expected rapid decay of magnetic fields under Ohmic diffusion. Studies have concluded that internal differential rotation in these celestial bodies can lead to magnetic field dissipation due to their typical turbulent nature. However, in objects with stable, differentially rotating magnetic fields that maintain axial symmetry, it has been found that stability can be preserved even in the presence of strong differential rotation. Additionally, these fields can be maintained when the internal dynamics of these objects lead to specific types of magnetic field stretching. Nevertheless, in objects with laminar internal turbulence, the stability of magnetic fields depends heavily on the field's topology and initial geometry. In contrast, in celestial bodies with complex turbulent fluctuations, the magnetic field decay rate is influenced by the level of turbulence and can be both inhibiting and accelerating, depending on the type of fluctuations. Ultimately, the discovery that the Intermittent Poincaré Recurrence Theorem can lead to reduced effective diffusion in highly conductive media with complex fluctuations has major implications for revising estimates of diffusion and turbulence-induced magnetic field decay rates.

The functional renormalization group (FRG) technique has been proven useful for analyzing complex systems in multiple disciplines, including statistical physics and quantum field theories, regardless of their complete analytical solutions. Despite its benefits, applying FRG to complex systems requires a balance between computational efficiency and level of detail, leading to various numerical implementations that vary in their level of detail. This paper introduces a straightforward numerical renormalization group approach that aims to bypass the issues associated with truncations used in the functional renormalization group by working directly with the full effective average action. By eliminating the need to deal with the rapidly changing singular trace term, the authors demonstrate the effectiveness of their algorithm and its potential to be further refined through the use of higher-order discretizations and adaptive time-stepping methods. The authors also discuss the relevance of their approach to quantum field theories in multiple dimensions and zero-dimensional models used to describe complex systems, including spin systems and bose gases, and highlight the potential for future research in these areas.

Music enthusiasts still heavily depend on conventional search engines like Google for pop music, which is surprising considering how indispensable the internet has become in everyday life. Our innovative proposal is for a music-centric search engine called Pied Piper, which will serve as a comprehensive meta-search tool, enabling users to find relevant music information by searching for lyrics, song metadata, audio, or a blend of any of these options.

This PhD research focuses on exploring specific geometric constructions over Lie groupoids and differential stacks. Building on the foundation of principal bundle theory, the study builds upon this knowledge by investigating the complexities of higher bundles, particularly those based on Lie n-groupoids. The underlying philosophy is to establish a corresponding theory for stacks, which mirrors the established theory of principal bundles. Furthermore, the research delves into the adaptations of connections and curvings on higher bundles, as well as the development of the concept of 'higher parallel transport,' leading to the introduction of a corresponding 2-field.

A statistical analysis of 1.3 mm continuum sources in the Dragon infrared dark cloud (IRDC) has been conducted using data from the Submillimeter Common-User Bolometer Array 2 (SCUBA-2) 1D Spectra. Dragon -256 represents a massive stellar nursery situated at the leading edge of the cloud, with observations revealing a 1.3 mm core mass function (CMF) that is still in its formation stage. The CMF exhibits a universal shape for 1.3 mm cores with a mass below 1000 solar masses, but deviates for lower masses. This deviation is thought to be a result of a size limit for star formation, with the core resolution in this study being approximately 2300 Astronomical Units. The deviation in the CMF mirrors a similar deviation in the observed 1.3 mm size distribution, with 83% of 1.3 mm sources being smaller than 0.31 millimeters in wavelength equivalent. This size limit is consistent with the diameter of the 1.3 mm emission in Dragon-256. The deviation in the CMF at lower masses may be a result of a detection bias, with more massive cores being more likely to extend beyond the resolution limit. Godel modal logics can be regarded as an extension of intutionistic modal logics with prelinearity. This study explores algebraic and relational semantics for Godel modal logics built upon the duality between finite Godel algebras and finite forests, a type of poset. The research considers subvarieties of basic Godel algebras with two modal operators, alongside their respective classes of finite relational frames, using Tarski-Herbrand-Godel duality. The study specifically examines the correspondence between post varieties and their relational semantics, with references to prior work on finite intuitionistic modal algebras.

LiDAR point clouds offer valuable measurements for complex environmental settings, enabling the development of machine learning algorithms to identify patterns and make predictions. This paper provides an overview of the latest research using LiDAR 3D point clouds for machine learning, covering topics from data preparation to active machine learning applications. The study also outlines preprocessing steps, feature extraction methods, classification techniques and explores how these algorithms are used in knowledge discovery and prediction tasks.

We examine a specific class of stationary random fields on a sphere, characterized by a covariance structure that follows an exponential pattern relative to the angular distance. This allows for the development of numerical methods that are both computationally efficient for calculating the cumulative distribution function and moments, and accurate. Our approach involves calculating the moments directly, which in turn enables us to derive high-precision approximations for the probability density function and cumulative distribution function using a nonparametric method. This method's effectiveness is demonstrated through our results, supported by additional findings that provide insights into the relationship between angular distance and expected values for various metrics, such as great-circle distance, surface area, and solid angle.

The source of ultra-high-energy cosmic rays (UHECRs) has remained a major puzzle in high-energy astrophysics for over half a century. To better understand UHECRs, researchers are employing multiple strategies, including a statistical analysis of the relationship between neutrinos and UHECRs to leverage the fact that neutrinos are more likely to be directed at our galaxy's center, thereby providing a better map for our journey to the Milky Way's core. To improve the reliability of this analysis, a revised dataset from the Pierre Auger Observatory has been used, which has removed outliers and produced a smoother relationship between the arrival directions of neutrinos and UHECRs. Subsequent analyses, including direction smoothing and the calculation of likelihood ratios, have yielded the most stringent limits on the relationship between the two until now.

The flow of complex liquids is significantly influenced by surface roughness, especially at interfaces. Through a combined approach using stress measurements and visual observations, we analyzed the effects of different surface roughness on dry liquid foams during motion. Our study shows that surfaces subjected to stick-slip motion during the movement of foams, experience high stress levels matching the internal pressure build-up. This stress breaks the surface into distinct patterns that correspond to the characteristic lengths of the foams' structure. The stress levels in our measurements also helped refine the understanding of the yield stress in dense liquid foams. The surface roughness induces a increase in the apparent yield stress of foams, which rises at a rate of 1/3 in relation to the magnitude of roughness. The study provides a surface-related parameter for describing the stress-buildup in complex liquids during movement, which shows signs of scaling. The insights gained from our analysis of foams can likely be applied to other particle-stabilized complex liquids.

This report details our methods that achieved top accuracy in identifying different types of skin cancer, using a dataset containing images of four categories: benign nevi, dermatosis, cancerous patches, and patches with uncertain classification. Notably, the dataset includes unbalanced data and challenges arising from the varying angles and lighting conditions in which the images were captured. Building on the work of previous researchers, we developed an innovative approach that achieved 99.55% accuracy, by integrating a deep learning technique called Inception v3 with a method to detect outliers based on entropy.

The steady-state behavior of an elastic membrane, situated between two fluids of differing densities in a rotating Hele-Shaw cell, subject to external pressure, is examined in a study that also compares its inextensibility to that of an extremely elastic membrane. When the inner fluid density surpasses the outer fluid density, the membrane exhibits a Rayleigh-Thomas instability due to centrifugal force, whereas gravity causes a reverse instability when the inner fluid density is lower. The rotation's angular velocity and the cell's parameters dictate whether the system experiences a fingering instability, causing the membrane to either become trapped in the gaps or form elastic branches extending into the outer fluid, akin to the Hele-Shaw instability observed in non-rotating cells under surface tension. The study investigates the conditions under which the membrane transitions from a trapped state to a state of finger formation, akin to the Snout instability seen in the subsurface erosion of salt domes due to seawater dissolution. The study reveals that the membrane becomes trapped when the angular velocity is below a critical value, directly proportional to the square root of the cell's rotation speed. The study finds that the number of elastic fingers is odd in regions of odd parity and even in regions of even parity. The number of fingers is proportional to the cube root of the angular velocity in high-rotation regimes. The study derives the finger spacing law, stating that the spacing is inversely proportional to the square root of the angular velocity. The study confirms its theoretical predictions

Building on a novel theory, microstate nonequilibrium thermodynamics, we've successfully applied it to examine the dynamics of systems undergoing expansion or contraction, despite a significant challenge. Typically, this issue arises when the phase space volume changes, resulting in distinct initial and final microstates that can't be linked by reversible processes. We present an innovative solution to overcome this limitation, using a system that undergoes free expansion without an external influence, and demonstrate that the proposed method aligns with thermodynamic principles. Our solution identifies the dissipated energy as a thermodynamic average of work performed by each individual microstate and confirms its nonnegative value during free expansion, which holds surprising implications.

Scientists have identified the presence of two specific isomers of ethynyl cyclopentadiene, e-C5H3-CCH and t-C5H3-CCH, in a dense molecular cloud called TMC-1 through a combination of observations and theoretical analysis. By making extensive use of observational data, researchers were able to determine the concentration of these isomers, while in laboratory experiments, they measured how these molecules interact with light across a broad frequency range. These interactions are crucial for understanding the chemical composition of TMC-1. By comparing the frequency of these interactions with the concentration of e-C5H3-CCH and t-C5H3-CCH, scientists were able to calculate the size of the area from which these molecules originate. This analysis also provides insights into the concentration of other compounds in TMC-1, such as T-C4H3, T-C6H5(CCH), and T-C6H5(CN), as well as into the relative abundance of CCH-containing compounds compared to CN-containing compounds.

In neural machine translation, the attention model is now an integral component, enabling selective focusing on source sentence parts to predict target words. However, research reveals that target word generation depends not only on source sentences, but also heavily on previous generated target words, including distant words that can be difficult to model using traditional recurrent neural networks. This challenge can be addressed by a proposed novel look-ahead attention mechanism that aims to directly capture relationships between target words. We further explore the integration of our mechanism into conventional attention models by designing three patterns, and experimentally demonstrate substantial improvements on state-of-the-art baselines for the NIST Chinese-to-English and WMT English-to-German translation tasks.

The significant discrepancy between advancing computational technology and real-world problem-solving led to a new field of study. Abramson and Parashar suggest that a parallel disparity in complex software and challenging practical applications calls for the emergence of translational computer science. From this viewpoint, we reexamine the development and implementation of grid computing. A translational perspective is helpful for comprehending the progress of grid computing technology. Specifically, we show how developing the grid computing infrastructure and the Globus Toolkit relied on innovative approaches that blended research and development. Furthermore, we suggest that future grid computing projects would benefit from explicitly considering a translational perspective.

A unified dark fluid concept, combining dark energy and dark matter into one component, can be described by both barotropic and complex decay parameters due to its inherent nature. This model, when applied to a flat universe, exhibits two phases of expansion, with its dynamics heavily influenced by its dissipative behavior. In the high-enormous equation of state limit, the model exhibits an exponential expansion, mirating the universe's present state, and our calculations confirm its stability and viability.

In educational settings, curiosity is a vital cognitive trait that fuels a learner's desire to acquire new knowledge. However, there is a lack of effective methods for measuring curiosity's development and spread within learning communities. This study proposes a groundbreaking approach that utilizes eye-tracking technology and social network analysis to examine how curiosity manifests and spreads in group learning environments by analyzing patterns in gaze behavior and understanding the underlying cognitive processes. Our research focuses on eye fixation duration as a measure of curiosity, identifying that novel information often generates curiosity through distinct patterns in where and how long eyes stay fixed on specific areas. Our findings show that curiosity is not only influenced by individual learning styles but also by the transfer of curiosity from one learner to another, leading to the emergence of highly curious individuals who play a crucial role in the overall dynamics of the learning community. Our research contributes to the field of education by providing a novel multimodal approach for measuring curiosity in group learning environments, setting the stage for the development of effective strategies to stimulate curiosity and enhance the overall potential of learning communities.

Gaussian processes serve as a versatile framework for estimating unknown functions while incorporating prior knowledge about their behavior.  While multiple Gaussian process implementations exist for standard domains, there's a lack of comparable alternatives for irregular, unstructured two-dimensional domains.  While some methods exist for such domains, they often entail a shift from the Gaussian process model to a different statistical framework.  In this paper, we introduce a distinct approach utilizing the Mat\'ern Gaussian process model and a well-established sampling technique, resulting in a direct method that maintains the Gaussian process model.  While this method is not a novel concept for regular grids, it becomes a highly efficient option for such settings, surpassing established irregular domain alternatives in computational speed for several test scenarios.  Furthermore, it demonstrates superior performance when applied to two-dimensional domains.

The effective management of urban roads in relation to traffic requires an ideal sensing system that can provide a comprehensive, real-time, and energy-efficient monitoring of drivers' movements and road conditions. To achieve this, we formulate an optimal sensing problem that determines the best way for a large number of ridesharing vehicles to coordinate their in-vehicle sensors to provide the most information-rich data to the urban management system. Traffic flow patterns are modeled using a variation of the Wardrop equilibrium principle, and the problem is framed within the context of a large-scale Markov decision process. By leveraging the equivalence between certain MDP formulations and optimal energy distribution on urban road networks, we develop a cooperative sensing strategy for vehicles and prove that our approach converges to a solution under specific conditions. Numerical simulations demonstrate the effectiveness of our scheme in reducing traffic congestion and the energy consumption of sensors.

Our research analyzes the implications of the J/ψ decay into visible gamma rays and invisible particles for field theories describing neutrinos, dark matter, and their interactions. By establishing stringent limits on heavy neutral current that affects J/ψ decay, we derive more rigorous constraints than those derived from J/ψ decay into hadronic pairs and invisible particles, affecting neutrino mass and the scale of effective field theories down to 5.9 TeV. These findings assume specific parameters and may have different implications for other effective field theories.

Previous variable stepsize Second Derivative General Linear Methods have already been implemented using the Runge-Kutta-Fehlberg approach. In this study, an extension is made to extend this concept to algebraic VSLGDLMs and VSDIMDLMs.

This work introduces multivariate functional singular spectrum analysis (MFSSA) across various dimensional domains, building on the foundations of multivariate singular spectrum analysis (MSSA). We offer a comprehensive framework consisting of theoretical underpinnings and a step-by-step implementation guide for the algorithm. Our research demonstrates the effectiveness of MFSSA through comparative studies of reconstruction accuracy in multivariate functional time series (MFTS) and real-world applications, including the analysis of intraday temperature curves and remote sensing images of vegetation. Additionally, MFSSA is made available through the Rfssa R package for user convenience.

Deep learning-based automated evaluation systems (AES) are increasingly used in recruitment, but they are often overtrusted and their decisions are rarely critically examined. To address this problem, the concepts of overstable and sensitive classifications have been introduced to evaluate the reliability of AIS systems. The growing prevalence of overtrusted AIS systems has been found to be associated with over sensitivity through various empirical validations and theoretical analyses. The ease with which a system's performance can be chance-fitted through adversarial inputs, as well as the emergence of the most over sensitive class, as indicators of the why behind this phenomenon have been explored. The risk of over stability leading to sudden system failures, as well as the over sensitivity causing severe biases and unfair outcomes, as potential consequences have been discussed. The design of more robust AIS systems through diversified loss functions, data augmentation techniques, and the incorporation of side information, as proposed solutions have been illustrated.

The power law decay $p(t,x) \sim t^{-\phi(x)}$ is commonly observed in the spatially dependent persistence probability $p(t,x)$ of the random walk $S = (S_t)_{t \ge 0}$ in one dimension, where $p(t,x)$ measures the likelihood that the random walk remains non-negative up to time $t$ while staying within the interval $(-x, x)$. This likelihood depends on the available phase space and is influenced by the position $x$. Notably, researchers have struggled to find a general formula $p(t,x)$ applicable to a wide range of intermediate values of $x$. In contrast, we introduce an easily computable quantity $p(t,x)$ through the use of bigram counts in a simple, discrete, and space-less weighted one-dimensional random walk. Our approach demonstrates that the bigram counts accurately reflect the expected counts and exhibits the desired properties, being independent of $t$ and $x$ while adhering to basic monotonicity conditions. Moreover, our solution maintains accuracy for an extended duration of time with high probability.

The ICRF test facility IShTAR at the Max-Planck Institute for Plasma Physics in Germany is designed to investigate how plasma interacts with radio frequency waves. A plasma source with a 0.1 meter diameter plasma area, a 0.4 meter length, and a 14 kW power level is built into the test facility. This plasma source, ICrF-1, is essential to the proper functioning of the facility. Previous studies of the plasma source have been conducted using a magnetic configuration in the closed flux mode, but there have also been findings of the open flux mode when specific start-up procedures are followed. A plasma source characterized using a combination of methods including Langmuir probes, a coherent cylindrical Langmuir diagnostic, and a linear Langmuir diagnostic has been found to exhibit the hallmarks of the open flux mode under certain conditions. A confirmation of the mode of the plasma source has been achieved by confirming the helicon mode through a detailed analysis of electron temperature, density, and flow velocity profiles. A confirmation of the helicon mode has been achieved by comparing experimental electron temperature and density data with theoretical calculations of the electron Hall fluid. A confirmation of the helicon mode has been further achieved by comparing electron flow velocity data with a combination of electron temperature and magnetic field data. In comparison to conventional chemical pesticides, microbial pesticides exhibit numerous advantages, which can be modelled through a system where entomopathogenic nematodes are used to eliminate and concurrently suppress the population of target insects. This system aims to manage pests through a continuous nematode release mechanism, where the model's equilibrium and Hopf bifurcation periodic solutions are analyzed for optimal pest control, which is further confirmed by numerical simulations and case studies.

The task of identifying and locating nuclei in histopathology images is crucial for various analysis tasks, yet it's a time-consuming and laborious process. Automating this process would greatly enhance efficiency, but current methods often produce unsatisfactory results. To address this challenge, we propose a novel, end-to-end nucleus detection framework, which produces bounding boxes around nuclei in histopathology images. Our proposed framework, called W-Net, consists of two components: a bounding box suggestion network and a refinement network. In the first stage, W-Net leverages existing object detection models to generate initial bounding boxes from histopathology images, thereby reducing the complexity of the subsequent stage. In the second stage, a unique convolutional operation is employed to expand the candidate points within each bounding box, allowing for more accurate detection of nuclei within the proposed boundaries. Experimental results on the DuPath-2016 dataset demonstrate that our model outperforms current state-of-the-art nucleus detection methods, achieving a mean average precision of 0.7444.

Let's consider a non-Archimedean local field of characteristic not two, denoted as F, and the Bessel or new Bessel representation of an odd special orthogonal group, denoted as SO(Q), or a symplectic group, denoted as Sp, and defined by a pair (Q, B), where B is a Bessel vector. The purpose of this paper is to demonstrate that for any two irreducible admissible representations, denoted as \sigma_1 and \sigma_2 of the group GL, if they differ only by their central character, and if both satisfy the condition that they are in the Bessel representation of (Q, B), then they will also satisfy the condition that they are in the new Bessel representation of (Q, B), thus implying that \sigma_1 being equivalent to \sigma_2.

Xiong and Liu previously provided a definition for graphs G that have hamiltonian n-th iterated line graphs, L^n(G), where n is 2 or greater. In this study, we examine whether an L^n(G) graph possesses a hamiltonian path, and offer a definition for G to achieve this condition. Additionally, we apply this definition to set multiple upper limits for a graph's hamiltonian path index.

Cell death due to pyroptosis, characterized by inflammation, can contribute to the high cytokine levels seen in severe cases of COVID-19.  Pyroptosis is primarily initiated through the NLRP3 inflammasome's activation, primarily as a response to the SARS-CoV-2 viral protease, 3CLpro.  Although 3CLpro triggers pyroptotic cell death, research has revealed its apoptotic potential as well, with the apoptotic effect being more beneficial in reducing inflammation.  Remdesivir has demonstrated the suppression of 3CLpro activity, hindering the virus's replication, and shown the induction of apoptosis in virus-infected cells, resulting in decreased cytokine levels.  To understand the complex interactions between NLRP3 inflammasome activation, pyroptosis, apoptosis and the release of inflammatory cytokines during SARS-CoV-2 infection, and to evaluate the potential apoptotic pyroptotic transition and the anti-inflammatory impacts of Remdesivir, a single-cell mathematical model was developed.  Parameter estimation and sensitivity analysis were conducted using Profile Likelihood and the gSobol algorithm respectively.  The single-cell NLRP3-driven model was later modified to incorporate the dual apoptotic pyroptotic cell death behavior and the Remdesivir-induced anti-inflammatory effects, thus allowing for the examination of the single-cell dynamics prior to, during and post-Remdesivir therapy.
